findings.title: Team admin/owner permission check uses `&&` instead of `||`
findings.body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`, so a user must satisfy both predicates at once. A team member who is only an admin (not the owner) is therefore rejected with FORBIDDEN, even though the UI exposes the "additional_guests" action and other checks in the codebase use `booking.isUserTeamAdminOrOwner` (an OR). In practice only the organizer (or an attendee) can add guests; team admins/owners operating on someone else's team booking get a confusing permission error. The two calls should be combined with `||`.

findings.title: Guest filters are case-sensitive, allowing blacklist bypass and duplicate attendees
findings.body: `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` is lowercased when parsed, but `uniqueGuests` compares `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` against the raw user input, and the duplicate check `guest === attendee.email` is also an exact string compare. Zod's `.email()` does not normalize case. As a result `Blocked@Example.com` passes the blacklist, and `John@x.com` creates a second attendee row next to an existing `john@x.com` (who then receives a duplicate invitation). Both comparisons should be done on lowercased values.

findings.title: Emails sent with unfiltered `guests` instead of `uniqueGuests`
findings.body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the raw request payload, but the DB write only used `uniqueGuests`. Inside `sendAddGuestsEmails` the check `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` decides whether someone gets a full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (new guest) or the `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` (existing attendee). Because already-existing attendees appear in `guests` whenever the caller resubmits them, those attendees get a full duplicate booking confirmation with a `METHOD:REQUEST` ICS instead of the "guests added" notice. Pass `uniqueGuests` here.

findings.title: Calendar sync uses the acting user's credentials, not the booking organizer's
findings.body: `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` builds the EventManager with the credentials of whoever called the mutation. The event being updated belongs to `booking.userId`. When a team admin/owner or an attendee (explicitly allowed by the permission check above) adds guests, the EventManager either has no calendar credentials at all (plain attendees) or only the actor's (admins), so `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` does not update the organizer's calendar event — guests are persisted in the DB and emailed, but never actually added to the calendar invite. Credentials for the booking's organizer/host should be used.

findings.title: Any attendee can add unlimited arbitrary email addresses
findings.body: The authorization check grants access to anyone whose email is in `booking.attendees`, and guests added by this same endpoint become attendees too. There is no cap on the number of addresses in `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` (`z.array(z.string().email())`) and no rate limiting, so a booker (or a guest they previously added) can repeatedly POST arbitrary addresses and cause cal.com to send them calendar invites and attendee emails from the organizer's identity — a spam/open-relay vector against arbitrary third parties. If attendees are meant to invite others, this needs at least a per-booking count limit and rate limiting, and probably a config flag.

findings.title: No validation of booking status before mutating attendees
findings.body: The handler loads the booking by id and only checks existence and permissions; it never checks `booking.status`. A direct API call can therefore add guests (and trigger calendar invites and emails) to a CANCELLED or REJECTED booking, resurrecting attendee records and sending invitations for an event that no longer takes place. The booking status should be validated (e.g. ACCEPTED/PENDING) before modifying attendees.

findings.title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores host/attendee email opt-outs
findings.body: Every other helper in this file consults `eventTypeDisableHostEmail(eventTypeMetadata)` / `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail(eventTypeMetadata)` before enqueuing emails, but `sendAddGuestsEmails` has no `eventTypeMetadata` parameter and unconditionally sends the organizer email (plus team members) and attendee emails. Event types configured with `disableStandardEmails.all.host` or `.attendee` will still send mail when guests are added, violating the organizer's explicit preference. The handler already loads `eventType`; its metadata should be passed through and checked here.

findings.title: No tests for the new addGuests endpoint or dialog
findings.body: The PR adds a new authenticated mutation that mutates attendee records, talks to calendar integrations and sends emails, plus a new dialog and a new form component, but contains no tests. The permission matrix (organizer / team admin / team owner / attendee / unrelated user), the dedupe and blacklist filtering, and the case where `updateCalendarAttendees` throws are exactly the kind of logic that regresses silently; at minimum a unit test for the handler's authorization and filtering would be expected.

findings.title: Error toast always shows raw tRPC code; fallback message is unreachable
findings.body: `const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`` always evaluates to a non-empty template string (e.g. `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR: <english text>`), so `message || t("unable_to_add_guests")` never falls back and users are shown internal error codes instead of the localized "Unable to add guests" text. Additionally `t(err.message)` only produces a translation when the server message happens to be a key; other messages are leaked verbatim.

findings.title: Hardcoded "Remove email" tooltip is not translated
findings.body: The remove button tooltip uses the literal string `content="Remove email"` instead of `t("remove_email")` / an existing locale key, while every other user-facing string in this component goes through `useLocale()`. In a fully localized product this surfaces English text in all non-English locales.
